newsitem.title: UK: C&W pays up for Panama but still eyes Europe.
newsitem.headline: C&W pays up for Panama but still eyes Europe.

text.p: Cable and Wireless on Wednesday won effective control of Panama's national telephone firm INTEL after a hefty $652 million bid -- but said the key markets of France and Germany remained a high priority in its strategy.

Chief executive Richard Brown confirmed that the company was still in alliance talks with America's AT & T Corp and the Global One partnership between Deutsche Telekom AG, France Telecom and America's Sprint Corp.
He also noted that other hopefuls wanted to partner C&W, Britain's second biggest telecoms group -- including Singapore Telecommunications Ltd and America's Bell Atlantic Corp and NYNEX Corp.
"So what to do? It's a nice problem to have," he told Reuters.

One, more pressing, problem is what will happen to one of C&W's main profit sources -- a near 60 percent stake in Hong Kong Telecommunications -- with only weeks to go before the British colony reverts to Chinese control.

Analysts say China may not be holding a gun to C&W's head. But they expect the group to "fight tooth and nail" to keep a stake of least 50 percent, but, given the strategic importance of telecommunications to China, C&W may have to reach a pragmatic decision.
Any further investment by the Chinese in Hong Kong Telecom is expected to be reciprocated with growth opportunities on the Chinese mainland -- but returns on such a venture are unproven.
The value of C&W's shares is underpinned by that of Kong Kong Telecoms' stock. "If the skids got under Hong Kong Telecom's shares, there's no reason to believe C&W will hold up," noted one analyst.
C&W shares were trading 8.5 pence weaker at 499.5p in afternoon business.

Industry experts do not expect any announcement about a global alliance before the cloud of uncertainty shrouding the future of Hong Kong Telecom has lifted -- and this could take three to four weeks, they say.

Brown noted that C&W, which has revenues of over 7.0 billion pounds ($11.6 billion) and which provides over 10 million customers in 50 countries with communications, was big enough in its own right to decide against a link-up with other groups.
"But if we join a global alliance, it has to make sense for us and the alliance that we may join -- and we are talking to a number of potential alliances," he said.

C&W's latest deal in Panama, through which it wins operational and management control in a booming telecoms market with only 12 percent line penetration, highlights the company's dislike of being a passive investor.
"We want to have substantial influence in the operations that we are a part of. (If not,) we're not going to bid -- or if we're in those, we are going to get out," Brown said.
C&W, which abandoned its German alliance with VEBA AG in February, denied market speculation that Global One -- its most hotly-tipped suitor -- had moved away from the British company.
"I don't see a door that's closed," Brown said.
A fresh territory in Panama, complete with the strategic importance of the canal, enhances C&W's position in the Caribbean/Central American markets with strong traffic flows to the U.S. and Far East.
Adrian Goodall at SBC Warburg welcomed the news that C&W had beaten America's GTE Corp in a bid which he said enhanced growth -- although at a full price.
"On 1996 profitability, the deal would both enhance earnings per share (by 0.4p to 28.4p in 1997/98) and reduce the EV/EBIDTA by 0.1 to 8.2 times," he said.
C&W paid $4,150 per line -- over 40 percent higher that GTE's bid and well above Panama government expectations.

But the value, considerable higher than the average European price of $1,500, is justified by higher growth rates -- and because of the low line penetration, most will be more profitable business clients, Goodall said. ($ = 0.604 British Pounds)
